overview: I developed the tools in this chapter to couple neural controllers to Gait2392, a human musculoskeletal model, and to mechanical models based on the computer-aided design (CAD) of our bipedal robot. Slow simulation and hand tuning in an earlier course project with Connor Morrow made it difficult to repeat the same experiment after changing the controller or the mechanical model. A scripted version of the walker in the MuJoCo physics engine made automatic tuning possible. The subsequent experiments use the human model, a robot counterpart with relocated muscle paths, and a model built from the lab robot's own geometry. I developed Simulink blocks and a graphical interface for building nonspiking circuits. A simulated knee reflex tests whether a sensory signal passes through a motor neuron and muscle to produce joint motion. The final experiments use scripts to tune controllers, test whether the feet alternate under load, and measure how much a faster neural calculation saves over a complete trial.
first_section: I built my first neuromechanical model in AnimatLab, a graphical program in which a neural circuit can activate muscles and receive sensory signals from the moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. For the course project, Morrow and I connected the circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} to the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. There is a passive toe joint. The legs made stepping-like movements while the model was suspended in air. When we lowered it to the ground and removed the support, the model fell over (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run, making a systematic search impractical.
